newsitem.title: USA: Deal to avert retrial of Orange County official.
newsitem.headline: Deal to avert retrial of Orange County official.

text.p: Orange County, California, prosecutors said Friday they reached an agreement with the county's former budget director that will avoid his retrial on felony charges stemming from the county's bankruptcy.

Assistant District Attorney Jan Nolan said former budget director Ronald Rubino, 44, has agreed to plead no contest to a single lesser charge that he falsified a county public record in violation of state law.
His sentence will be 100 hours of community service and two years of unsupervised probation, Nolan said.

After Rubino pleads no contest to the new charge, the District Attorney will drop two existing felony counts against him, Nolan said. These more serious charges carried a maximum penalty of nine years in state prison.
Superior Court Judge J. Stephen Czuleger was expected to approve the agreement at a hearing in Santa Ana Monday.

"I think it's equitable," Nolan said of the deal with Rubino. "Our goal was to place accountability and responsibility on these public officials and the fact that he's pleading no contest to this felony charge, in our mind, achieves our goal of demanding accountability."

In a letter to the southern California county's Board of Supervisors, Rubino continued to assert his innocence of any charges. He said it was in the best interest of his family, friends and the public to put an end to "this ordeal."

In a no contest plea, a defendant does not admit guilt but states he or she will offer no defense. The person is then subject to being judged guilty and punished as if he or she had pleaded guilty or had been convicted.
Nolan said Rubino will be able to petition the court at the end of the first year of his probation to withdraw his no contest plea and enter a plea of innocent. The charge will then be dismissed.

Rubino was indicted by a county grand jury in December 1995 on two felony charges accusing him of helping former county Treasurer Robert Citron divert funds from other government agencies for the county's benefit.
His trial, the first criminal trial to arise from the county bankruptcy, began in August but ended in a mistrial Sept. 13. A new trial had been set to begin next week.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy protection on Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining investment losses of more than $1.6 billion. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
